title: Retries, Circuit Breakers & Backpressure
summary: Production systems fail constantly — networks blip, dependencies slow down, disks fill up. Reliability patterns prevent small failures from cascading into outages. Retries recover transient errors, circuit breakers stop calling broken services, bulkheads isolate blast radius, and backpressure prevents overload.

sections.title: Designing for Failure
paragraphs: Every dependency will fail eventually: databases, payment gateways, third-party APIs, DNS, the network itself. Reliability engineering assumes failure is normal and designs systems to degrade gracefully rather than collapse entirely.

The goal is not zero failures — it is bounded impact, fast recovery, and predictable degradation. Users may see slower responses or reduced features, but the core service stays available. SLOs (Service Level Objectives) define acceptable failure budgets.

Reliability patterns are implemented in application code, client libraries (gRPC retries), service meshes (Istio circuit breaking), and infrastructure (load shedder, rate limiters). Consistency across services matters — one service without timeouts can hang an entire call chain.

sections.title: Retries, Timeouts, and Jitter
paragraphs: Retries recover from transient failures: network timeouts, 503 responses, connection resets. Always combine retries with timeouts — a retry without a timeout can wait forever. Set deadlines per request and per call chain.

Exponential backoff increases delay between retries (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s) to give failing services time to recover. Jitter adds randomness to prevent synchronized retry storms — without jitter, thousands of clients retry simultaneously and re-overwhelm the recovering service.

Retry only idempotent operations unless using idempotency keys. POST /charge without an idempotency key must not blind retry — you may double-charge. GET, PUT with idempotency keys, and DELETE are safer retry candidates.

sections.title: Circuit Breakers
paragraphs: A circuit breaker wraps calls to a dependency and tracks failure rates. Closed (normal): calls pass through. Open (tripped): calls fail fast without hitting the dependency — return fallback or error immediately. Half-open: allow a probe request to test recovery.

Circuit breakers prevent cascading failures. When the payment service is down, the order service stops hammering it, returns a graceful error, and preserves threads and connection pools for healthy paths.
Netflix Hystrix popularized this pattern; today Resilience4j, Polly, and service meshes provide implementations. Configure failure thresholds, reset timeouts, and fallbacks per dependency.

sections.title: Bulkheads, Rate Limiting, and Load Shedding
paragraphs: Bulkheads isolate resources — separate thread pools or connection pools per dependency so one slow service cannot exhaust all threads. Named after ship compartments that contain flooding.

Rate limiting protects services from overload: token bucket and sliding window algorithms cap requests per client or globally. Return 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After header. Rate limit at the edge (API gateway) and at critical internal services.

Load shedding drops requests when the system is overloaded — prefer rejecting new work over failing all in-flight requests. Prioritize critical paths (checkout) over background jobs (recommendations).

sections.title: Backpressure
paragraphs: Backpressure signals upstream producers to slow down when downstream consumers cannot keep pace. Without backpressure, buffers grow unbounded until memory exhaustion — the slow consumer problem.
Reactive streams (Project Reactor, RxJava), gRPC flow control, and Kafka consumer pause/resume implement backpressure. TCP itself applies backpressure via window sizes.
In queue-based systems, monitor queue depth and scale consumers or throttle producers when depth exceeds thresholds. Unbounded queues are a reliability anti-pattern.

deepDive.title: Retries, Circuit Breakers & Backpressure — Operational deep dive
paragraphs: Operating Retries, Circuit Breakers & Backpressure well means defining the scarce resource (CPU, memory, disk, network, or tokens), the SLIs that reflect user pain, and the knobs that trade cost for latency.
Under load, measure amplification: how many bytes, RPCs, or disk writes you pay per user request. Prefetch and batch only when measurements show benefit — premature batching adds tail latency.
Failure drills should include dependency slowdown (not only hard down), clock skew, and disk full. Verify alerts, dashboards, and runbooks against those drills.
bullets: Name the scarcest resource and budget it
Track p50/p99 and error rate for the user journey

deepDive.title: Retries, Circuit Breakers & Backpressure — Correctness edges
paragraphs: Correctness edges around Retries, Circuit Breakers & Backpressure often appear at retries, partial writes, and schema evolution. Make handlers idempotent and state transitions explicit.

Document what clients may observe during failover: stale reads, duplicate messages, or delayed visibility. If the product cannot tolerate an anomaly, enforce a stronger consistency boundary — and pay for it knowingly.

expert.title: Retries, Circuit Breakers & Backpressure — Expert / multi-region notes
paragraphs: At multi-region scale, Retries, Circuit Breakers & Backpressure interacts with RTT, quorum placement, and cost of cross-region replication. Prefer region-local user paths with asynchronous global state when invariants allow.
Cost envelopes matter: chart unit cost vs QPS and vs data size. Many 'performance' projects are actually cost projects in disguise — make the objective explicit.

concepts: Exponential backoff with jitter for retries
Timeouts and deadlines on every outbound call
Circuit breaker states: closed, open, half-open
Bulkheads: isolated resource pools per dependency
Rate limiting: token bucket, sliding window, leaky bucket
Load shedding: drop low-priority work under pressure
Backpressure: slow producers when consumers lag
Idempotency keys for safe retries on mutations
Cascading failure and failure domain isolation
practices: Set timeouts on every HTTP, gRPC, and database call — no exceptions
Use retry with exponential backoff + jitter; cap max attempts
Implement circuit breakers on all external dependencies
Use idempotency keys for payment, order, and booking operations
Rate limit public APIs and expensive internal endpoints
Monitor error rates, latency p99, and circuit breaker state per dependency
Load test failure scenarios — kill dependencies and observe cascade behavior
pitfalls: Retrying without jitter during an outage — amplifies the failure
Unbounded retries on non-idempotent POST requests
No timeout — one hung dependency blocks all worker threads
Circuit breaker thresholds too sensitive — flapping open/closed
Unbounded queues masking consumer failure until OOM
Fallback that returns stale or incorrect data without user indication

examples.title: Payment service circuit breaker
examples.description: Order service wraps payment API calls in a circuit breaker. After 5 failures in 10 seconds, circuit opens — orders queue for later payment retry and users see 'payment processing.' Half-open after 30 seconds probes one request. Success closes circuit; failure reopens.

examples.title: Retry storm without jitter
examples.description: A DNS blip causes 500 errors. Ten thousand clients retry simultaneously every second with fixed 1s backoff. The recovering service is immediately overwhelmed again. Adding full jitter spreads retries over a window, allowing recovery.

examples.title: Kafka backpressure
examples.description: A consumer processing messages slower than production rate accumulates lag. Consumer pauses partition fetching when internal buffer is full — applying backpressure to the broker. Alert fires on lag > 100K; autoscaler adds consumer instances.

keyTakeaways: Assume every dependency fails — design for graceful degradation
Retries need backoff, jitter, timeouts, and idempotency
Circuit breakers fail fast and prevent cascade overload
Bulkheads and rate limits contain blast radius
Backpressure prevents unbounded buffering and OOM
Test failure modes — reliability patterns must be verified under chaos
whyItMatters: Major outages at cloud providers and financial institutions often trace to missing timeouts, retry storms, or absent circuit breakers — not exotic bugs. These patterns are the difference between a blip and a multi-hour incident. They appear in every system design discussion about production readiness.
reflectionQuestions: What happens if retries do not use jitter during a widespread outage?
How does a circuit breaker differ from a simple timeout?
When should you not retry a failed request?
How would you implement backpressure in a synchronous REST API?
